The tuba is the lowest voice of the brass family. As on every brass instrument, your **lips buzz** in a cup-shaped mouthpiece. This page follows a teacher's resource book
(see the Works Cited), in this site's own words. The book's pages on the tuba's history and family are not in the scan this page was made from, so **those are left out**.
For the fingerings (BB♭ tuba and sousaphone, E♭ tuba, treble clef) go to the [Trumpet, Euphonium and Tuba fingering charts](brass-fingerings.qmd).

## The parts {#parts}

The book labels a three-valve tuba: the **mouthpiece**, **mouthpiece receiver**, **lead pipe**, **bell**, **body**, **valves 1, 2, 3**, the **first, second and third valve slides** and the **main tuning slide**.
It also draws the **sousaphone**, the same low brass wrapped around the player's body for marching.

## Putting it together and sitting {#posture}

**Assembly.** Put the mouthpiece in the receiver on the lead pipe and give it a **gentle twist**, not too tight.

**Posture and hands.**

1. Sit **up straight at the edge of the chair**, feet flat on the floor.
2. **Rest the tuba on your lap** so that the **bottom "U"** of the instrument sits on your **thighs**. Hold the body with your **left arm**.
3. Put your **right thumb in the ring**, if the tuba has one.
4. Put the **tips of your first three fingers** on the valve buttons; the right hand makes a relaxed **"C"**, as if holding a tennis ball.
5. Keep your **wrists straight** and your **elbows away from your body**.

## Your embouchure and first sound {#embouchure}

1. **Wet your lips** and shape your mouth and throat as if saying **"oh"**. Bring the lips together as if saying **"em"**.
2. Take a **full breath through the mouth** and blow through closed lips: a **relaxed buzz**.
3. Hold the mouthpiece by the **shank**, set it **over the middle of the buzz** with equal amounts on the upper and lower lip, **without much pressure**. Check in a **mirror**.
4. Breathe in fully and play a **long, steady buzz** on the mouthpiece.

## When the tone goes wrong {#tone-problems}

| What you hear | Possible causes | Try this |
|---|---|---|
| 1. No tone, rushing air | embouchure not firm enough; blowing, not buzzing; air stream restricted (closed throat, high tongue) | re-form with a **smaller opening** and firm up; buzz without the mouthpiece; say "oh" to open the throat and keep the tongue down |
| 2. Thin, pinched tone | embouchure too tight; too little air between the lips | re-form with a **larger opening** and relax; breathe deeply and push the air out fast |
| 3. Garbled tone | embouchure not firm enough; lips folding over the teeth | smaller opening and firm up; re-form and use the mouthpiece ring to check lip position |
| 4. Stopped or intense air | lips pinched shut; too little air between the lips | relax; check the tongue with "oh" and use faster air |

## Tuning {#tuning}

- **Tone first**: "you can't tune a poor tone".
- **Slur up to a tuning note** (the book prints one for beginners and one for more advanced players, both in bass clef, the advanced one ending on a B♭).
  **Sharp**: pull the main tuning slide **out**. **Flat**: push it **in**. Then tune each **valve slide** on a note that uses that valve. A small main-slide change should not need new valve-slide settings.

## Daily care {#care}

**Putting it away.** Press the **water key** and **blow** (not buzz) to empty the water. **Wipe** the tuba with a soft, clean cloth. **Push in all slides**, pressing the matching valve each time. Take out the mouthpiece
and put both in the case. **Latch** it.

**Oiling piston valves (daily).** Unscrew **only the first valve** at the top of its casing (not the button) and do not touch the part the casing protects. Put **5 or 6 drops** of valve oil along the metal part with the holes.
**Line up the valve guide with its groove** as you put it back. Push the button up and down quickly. Repeat with the other valves.

**Greasing the slides (regularly).** One slide at a time, with its valve pressed (the main tuning slide needs no valve): wipe off old grease, apply a **generous** amount of new grease,
put the slide back, **work it in and out**, push it in and wipe off the extra, and repeat with the others.

**Rotary valves.** Some tubas have rotary valves.

- *Daily:* remove **one valve slide** as if emptying water (press the matching lever). Turn the tuba so the slide opening that joins the body faces the **ceiling**. Put **3 or 4 drops** of rotary or valve oil in the hole,
  working the lever up and down. Turn the tuba back and put the slide back (lever pressed). Do all the valves.
- *Often:* take off the **valve cap** at the top or bottom (depending on the model), without touching the exposed valve. Put **one drop** on the small raised circle of the valve, put the cap back,
  and move the valve up and down quickly. Also a drop on each **valve stem**.

## Brass checklist {#checklist}

Sitting straight, head up, left hand and wrist, right hand and wrist, instrument placed right for your body, fingers gently curved, elbows away, mouthpiece in the right place,
corners of the lips firm and the centre relaxed, chin flat and pointed, breathing well, relaxed buzz.
